meta.data_status: PLACEHOLDER — invented ranking in the real schema shape. Replace with the merged team Top-10 before the demo.

scoring.method: Sum of five criteria, each scored 0-20 (max 100).

criteria.label: Essentiality
criteria.meaning: How lethal or crippling is loss of function?

criteria.label: Specificity
criteria.meaning: How divergent from bees, pollinator weevil, parasitoid wasps and vertebrates?

criteria.label: RNAi evidence
criteria.meaning: Published knockdown phenotype in this or a related species.

criteria.label: Annotation confidence
criteria.meaning: BLAST identity/coverage plus InterPro domain agreement.

criteria.label: Druggability
criteria.meaning: Existing chemistry, or a tractable binding site.

meta.notes: Every candidate is also present in proteins.json with the same protein_id. The detail modal can render either record with one function.

candidates.annotation: V-type proton ATPase catalytic subunit A
candidates.mechanism: Acidifies the midgut lumen. Knockdown collapses gut ion transport and nutrient uptake, which is lethal rather than merely sub-lethal.
candidates.why_selected: The strongest combination of certain lethality and a delivery route that already works: larvae feed constantly on frond tissue, so oral dsRNA reaches the midgut epithelium where this gene is most expressed.
candidates.literature_support: dsRNA knockdown reported lethal in several lepidopteran and coleopteran pests.

specificity.off_target_method: 21-nt sliding window vs beneficial-insect transcriptomes using genes_nucleotide.fasta
specificity.notes: Protein is conserved, so selectivity has to come from nucleotide-level dsRNA design rather than the protein itself.

risks: Conserved across insects — dsRNA sequence choice does all the selectivity work.
candidates.next_step: Design three 200-300 bp dsRNA windows in the least conserved regions, then run the off-target screen.

candidates.mechanism: ESCRT-III component required for endosomal sorting. Knockdown blocks membrane protein turnover and kills larvae slowly but reliably.
candidates.why_selected: The most commercially validated insect dsRNA target in existence, and short enough that the whole coding sequence can be scanned for a species-narrow dsRNA window.
candidates.literature_support: Basis of the first approved RNAi trait in a commercial crop (western corn rootworm).

specificity.notes: Nucleotide divergence between lepidopteran snf7 genes is high enough to design narrow-spectrum dsRNA.

risks: Slow kill speed — plantation managers expect visible knockdown within days.
candidates.next_step: Confirm the Metisa sequence differs from Elaeidobius kamerunicus snf7 across every 21-nt window.

candidates.mechanism: Polymerises the chitin of new cuticle at each moult. Knockdown produces lethal moulting failure with the larva trapped mid-ecdysis.
candidates.why_selected: Insect and fungal enzyme with no vertebrate counterpart, so the whole pathway is intrinsically selective. Benzoylurea chemistry already attacks it, which means the biology is proven in the field.
candidates.delivery_strategy: Oral dsRNA, or small-molecule inhibitor building on benzoylureas
candidates.literature_support: RNAi and benzoylurea inhibition both give moulting lethality across Lepidoptera.

specificity.notes: No vertebrate orthologue — the strongest structural selectivity argument in the set.

risks: Also present in beneficial insects, so dsRNA windows still need screening.
candidates.next_step: Check whether the Metisa gene has the CHS-A specific alternative exon used for isoform-selective targeting.

candidates.notes: Best-identity hit in split 3 (~94% to Spodoptera, Papilio, Mythimna). Evidence the proteome is clean and on-target.
candidates.mechanism: Propagates the nerve action potential and is the binding site of pyrethroids and DDT. Modulation causes rapid paralysis.
candidates.why_selected: The only candidate that delivers immediate knockdown speed, and our own split-3 BLAST recovered it at ~94% identity to three other moths — the cleanest annotation in the whole dataset.
candidates.delivery_strategy: Small-molecule modulator; also the reference point for monitoring kdr resistance mutations
candidates.literature_support: Established target site of the pyrethroid class; kdr/super-kdr mutations are well characterised.

specificity.off_target_method: Sequence alignment of the pyrethroid binding pocket vs Apis mellifera and Elaeidobius kamerunicus
beneficial_conflicts: Highly conserved in bees — the weakest selectivity score in the Top-10
specificity.notes: Selectivity would have to come from pocket-level differences, not overall divergence.

risks: Field resistance to this site already exists in other pests.
candidates.next_step: Scan our sequence for known kdr positions to see whether resistance alleles are already present in Malaysian populations.

candidates.mechanism: Heterodimerises with USP to switch on the moulting gene cascade. Both agonists and knockdown block metamorphosis.
candidates.why_selected: A single control point for the entire moulting programme, and diacylhydrazine chemistry shows lepidopteran-selective agonism is achievable.
candidates.literature_support: Diacylhydrazines are selectively active on lepidopteran EcR; RNAi blocks moulting.

specificity.off_target_method: Ligand-binding domain alignment across Hymenoptera and Coleoptera
beneficial_conflicts: Present in parasitoid wasps — timing of application matters
specificity.notes: No vertebrate orthologue. Order-level selectivity is documented for existing agonists.

risks: Parasitoid wasps share the pathway, so spray timing must avoid their larval stages.
candidates.next_step: Model the ligand-binding pocket against known diacylhydrazine-sensitive residues.

candidates.mechanism: Converts chitin to chitosan in the new cuticle laminae. Knockdown gives fragile, disorganised cuticle and death at ecdysis.
candidates.why_selected: Same selectivity logic as chitin synthase but a smaller, better-behaved gene for dsRNA design, and it sits downstream so it is less likely to be compensated.
candidates.literature_support: CDA1/CDA2 knockdown causes moulting defects in several lepidopterans.

specificity.notes: No vertebrate orthologue; moderate identity to other moths suggests usable nucleotide divergence.

risks: Family has partially redundant members (CDA2 onward).
candidates.next_step: Count how many CDA paralogues exist in the full 26,490 proteome before committing.

candidates.mechanism: Calcium release channel of muscle. Diamide binding causes uncontrolled calcium leak, then paralysis and feeding arrest.
candidates.why_selected: Insect RyR is different enough from the vertebrate channel to give genuine mammalian safety, and diamides already prove the site is druggable.
candidates.literature_support: Target of chlorantraniliprole and flubendiamide; G4946E resistance mutation characterised in diamondback moth.

specificity.off_target_method: Transmembrane domain alignment vs vertebrate RyR1-3 and Apis mellifera
beneficial_conflicts: Some hymenopteran sensitivity reported for diamides
specificity.notes: Selectivity is pocket-level, and it is already commercially demonstrated.

risks: 5,210 aa gene — hard to assemble and validate confidently.
candidates.next_step: Check our sequence at the known diamide-resistance positions.

candidates.mechanism: Midgut brush-border receptor that Bt Cry toxins bind before pore formation. Loss of APN1 is a known route to Bt resistance.
candidates.why_selected: Directly addresses the problem in the brief — Bt is already failing on this pest. Characterising APN1 explains why, and points at a way to restore Bt efficacy.
candidates.delivery_strategy: Diagnostic marker plus Cry protein re-engineering, not a kill target itself
candidates.literature_support: APN1 downregulation and mutation both linked to Cry1Ac resistance in Lepidoptera.

specificity.notes: Large paralogue family in Lepidoptera — the specific member matters.

risks: Knocking it down could increase Bt resistance rather than reduce it — mechanism must be stated carefully in the report.
candidates.next_step: Resolve which APN paralogue this is by building the APN family tree (MAFFT + IQ-TREE).

candidates.mechanism: Oxidises pyrethroids and neonicotinoids. Silencing does not kill, it restores susceptibility to insecticides the pest currently survives.
candidates.why_selected: The clearest resistance-breaker in the set. Paired with an existing insecticide it converts a failing product back into a working one, which is cheaper than developing new chemistry.
candidates.delivery_strategy: dsRNA co-formulated as a synergist with existing insecticide
candidates.literature_support: CYP6AE members repeatedly implicated in metabolic resistance in noctuid pests.

specificity.off_target_method: 21-nt sliding window vs beneficial-insect transcriptomes; CYP6 family is fast-evolving so divergence is expected
specificity.notes: Insect-specific subfamily — the fast evolution that makes P450s hard to name also makes them easy to target narrowly.

risks: Not lethal on its own — must be sold as a synergist.
Detox P450s are redundant, so several members may need silencing together.
candidates.next_step: Cluster all split-3 P450s into subfamilies to see how many CYP6AE paralogues we actually have.

candidates.annotation: ATP-binding cassette transporter subfamily C member 2
candidates.mechanism: Effluxes xenobiotics and also acts as a Cry toxin receptor. Mutations here are one of the best-documented causes of Bt resistance.
candidates.why_selected: Completes the resistance story alongside CYP6AE and APN1: efflux, metabolism, and receptor loss are the three ways this pest survives what we spray.
candidates.literature_support: ABCC2 loss-of-function confers Cry1Ac resistance in multiple lepidopteran species.

specificity.notes: Coverage is only 84% — worth confirming the gene model is complete before relying on it.

risks: Partial coverage suggests a possibly truncated gene prediction.
Same caution as APN1: silencing it may mimic resistance.
candidates.next_step: Re-check the gene model boundaries against the nucleotide FASTA.
